item.title: Rethinking ADHD Study Habits
item.description:
ADHD

Rethinking ADHD Study Habits

Why your child with ADHD may need change, not just structure.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • Novelty grabs your attention, which is why it’s an essential tool for managing homework challenges in ADHD.
  • Neural resets are a strategy for keeping novelty in the workflow.
  • Embrace flexibility, as routines are helpful but not sufficient to keep the ADHD brain from checking out.

I sat in the Boston University library, on the fourth floor, and I counted out the M&Ms—10 of them—placing them on a piece of paper in the corner of the desk. I stood up and stretched before returning to the pictures of parasites in eyeballs. I looked at my watch, anticipating my sweet treat in about 30 minutes, and then I dug into my work. I had friends in medical school who could study for hours without moving, and I used to wonder what was wrong with me. Eventually I realized I just had to be kind to myself and do what worked. I studied in different places, changed subjects frequently, and sometimes worked backwards from the end of a chapter to the beginning. Years later, I would know about my ADHD diagnosis, but at the time I just knew I had to study differently than my peers.

Keeping me on task.
Source: Tomoya606/Shutterstock

What do all these things have in common—why did they help with my ADHD brain? One word: novelty. ADHD nervous system circuits need high intensity to get going and stay moving. They get bored quickly. Study strategies that weave novelty into the workflow are powerful. This can seem counterintuitive when ADHD coaching often centers on structure, routine, and predictability—but without including novelty, these ideas often work for a while and then fade out.

How can you use this principle to support your child or teen with ADHD in their approach to homework and studying this school year?

Work in small, flexible chunks of time

Workable and successful time frames will vary by age, task, and personal factors. Whether it's five minutes for a third grader or 30 minutes for a high school junior, planning small, achievable periods helps overcome the paralysis of facing a task that seems massive. And keep in mind that the 8-year-old may spend an hour on something that fascinates her, and the high school junior may be so tired on a particular day that the five-minute chunk may be all he can muster. The details will vary but the strategy builds the foundation.

Even if your child can hyperfocus for hours, breaks are essential to prevent cognitive fatigue and help them manage the "Mt. Everest" feeling of upcoming work. Brains and bodies get tired and stiff. Learning becomes far less productive if you go past a certain point of cognitive fatigue.

Strategic rewards

A tasty snack, a walk outside, or a short game can be good break-time activities. Avoid screens when possible, as they are hard to disengage from, but prioritize movement and activities your child finds inherently interesting. Some families and kids love a good dance party break. Don’t suggest a run on the treadmill or practicing the piano unless those are really fun things for your child. This isn’t about more productivity—it’s about planful rest and fun to reset the nervous system.

article continues after advertisement
Dance parties can be a fun study break
Source: Fizzes/Shutterstock

Make room for flexible study spaces

While a dedicated study area is a common recommendation, it may be that a child or teen with ADHD needs to move around the house and study in different places to maintain novelty. Let them. See if they want to create a movable “study kit” with required supplies that they can pick up and move with them. This might include pens/pencils/extra paper/an extra charging cord/fidgets or whatever they need.

Adapt to the flow of quiet vs. a soundtrack for studying

Some children and teens need total quiet to study and do homework while others need background noise or sounds. Parents’ “excuse” alarm often goes off when kids say they need sound to study, but it’s a common ADHD brain quirk and worth giving a try. Noise-canceling headphones can be a great investment so your child can tune out when they need quiet or tune into their background sounds when they need them. Best choices for background content are things that are familiar—not novel—such as favorite music, previously read and loved audiobooks, or shows/videos they have watched 100 times. Keep the cellphone out of sight, though, as even turned off, they can be very distracting.

Studying in the kitchen with others around can work!
Source: AnnaStills/Shutterstock

Consider the need for and value of body-doubling

Many children and teens (and adults) with ADHD struggle to work independently—having someone else around helps with focus. Your child may want to be around you or others while studying, even if they don’t need help with the work itself (although they may need that too). Try to be patient with your child who plops themselves in the middle of the busy kitchen to get work done or who keeps coming out of their room or who calls out to you with seemingly unnecessary questions just to get you to come in. Just being in the same room or sitting next to them while you read or do something else may be a big help.

article continues after advertisement

Shake the brain up and work backward or from the middle

Work backward or from the middle. Tackling math problems, vocabulary lists, or a short-answer question sheet from the end to the beginning or jumping into the middle can shake up the brain, providing needed novelty. Even with text reading, jumping ahead to the end can sometimes be an interesting tactic—getting to the “why” without wading through all the “what.”

Follow curiosity

Stopping to look up an interesting word or person may seem like a distraction, but it often adds depth to monotonous tasks and provides a necessary novelty break.

Embrace flexibility: Work with the brain and not against it

Understand that your child’s needs may change depending on the day or the subject. Trust their feedback on what environment helps them focus.

Sleep is more important than homework

While not specific to novelty, I never miss an opportunity to say this. Sleep is the ultimate break. If work isn't finished by bedtime, put it away. Your child needs rest far more than they need to finish every assignment. Tomorrow is a new day.

item.title: Why 'Work-Life Balance' Is a Myth—and What to Do Instead
item.description:
Career

Why 'Work-Life Balance' Is a Myth—and What to Do Instead

As we go back to school, how we should really manage “work-life balance."

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • Work-life balance suggests there's a finish line.
  • Harmony between the demands of our life is a better concept.
  • Energy management is a key skill to managing our varying life demands.
The elusive "work-life" balance.
Source: Myles Bloomfield/Unsplash

In my work, I generally dislike the concept of "work-life balance" for several reasons. First, it treats work and life as opposites. But increasingly for many people, these two intermingle. There is no clear ability to separate the two. If you’ve ever had a call from your child’s school while at work or had a work email or call show up while spending time with your family, you know that the days of keeping these things separate are no longer. Second, the idea of “balance" suggests that these two aspects are sitting on either end of a scale, and the goal is to get them level and keep them there. That image implies a finish line. But there is never a “finish line” when it comes to managing these aspects of life. They constantly change and we must constantly adjust. So the idea that we can find a perfect “balance” makes for an unrealistic goal. In sum, the idea of “work-life balance” is nonsense. So what should we focus on instead?

A better word is harmony, not balance

Harmony isn't about getting opposites to balance out. It's about getting the different demands of your life to work together reasonably well. It highlights that there is a fluidity and change to the different aspects of our life. And the most important issue in trying to get these aspects of life to work together is your energy allocation. Thus, the real question isn't, "How do I balance work and life?" It's, "How do I allocate my time and energy across the things competing for them right now?" That's a different problem to solve, and a much more useful one.

Energy isn't unlimited

It’s a terrible thing we have done in our culture to suggest that if you just try harder, you can get done everything on your to-do list. It makes it seem that if we aren’t handling all the demands, it's because we’re not trying hard enough. More often than not, the demands are unrealistic for the energy we have. The reality is that our energy is fixed and we cannot magically create more energy through willpower. A more accurate concept is to imagine our energy like a battery. It can be charged and drained and there is a fixed amount.

The real skill to learn

In the training I run on this, we don't start with time management. We start with energy management and these three key pieces:

  1. Being more mindful about what actually charges and drains your battery. While there are some drains that are consistent for everyone, there are real individual differences in our charges and drains that are useful to pay attention to. What are the charges and drains in your day?
  2. Being more intentional about charging our battery. I bet you put some effort today into charging your cellphone. You noticed it was low and found a charger. When’s the last time you were intentional about charging your own battery? There are some very effective ways to charge our battery and there are some things we do that we sometimes think are charging us but they are actually energy drains in disguise (social media, I’m looking at you). What activities you feel more energetic at the end than when you started? This isn't about healthy habits. It's about things that make you smile.
  3. Choosing how to spend our limited battery. This goes directly to the work-life balance issue. How do you decide how to spend your limited battery? And what do you do when your battery isn’t enough for the real demands of your life? What can only you do and what could anyone do? How can you add extra batteries to the system?
article continues after advertisement

Finally, we don’t just focus on "what" you should do around battery management, but also "how" to do it. There are a lot of tips and tricks from psychological science that can make building these habits a lot more effective. “Try harder” is not an evidence-based strategy for building habits.

As you get ready for returning to school this year, consider how to manage your battery and how to get the demands of your life working in harmony instead of the elusive "work-life balance."
